**Client relationship management (CRM)** is the set of habits and records you use to look after people who already buy from you, so that they stay, buy again and recommend you. The word CRM is also used for software such as HubSpot or Zoho, but the habits come first. A tailor with a good notebook and a steady follow-up routine is doing CRM. A business with expensive software that nobody updates is not.

This course is for women who already have some clients: a caterer, a hairdresser, a tutor, a bookkeeper, a soap maker who supplies shops, a virtual assistant. If you are still learning how to talk to a new buyer, handle objections or recover from a complaint, the WODDI course **Customer Relations and Sales** covers that. Here we focus on what happens after the first sale: records, follow-ups, expectations, repeat orders and service history.

The five stages of the client lifecycle
**Enquiry:** she asks a question, sees your Status, or is referred by a friend.
**Onboarding:** you agree what she is buying, the price, the deposit and the date. This is where expectations are set.
**Delivery:** you do the work or hand over the goods, and record what was delivered.
**After-care:** a short check that she is happy, a care tip, a thank-you. Most small businesses skip this stage.
**Repeat and referral:** she orders again, or sends someone to you. The cycle starts again, usually faster and with more trust.

Look at where clients drop out. If many people enquire but few pay, your problem is earlier, in selling. If people buy once and disappear, the gap is usually after-care and follow-up, which is exactly what this course fixes.
Why a returning client is worth more

A new client costs you time and often money before she pays anything: answering questions, sending pictures, maybe paying for adverts or transport to meet her. A returning client already trusts your quality and your prices, so the conversation is shorter. She also tends to need fewer explanations, pays more readily and forgives a small delay because she knows your record. You do not need a published statistic to see this. Count it in your own business.

The simplest way to put a number on a relationship is **client lifetime value**: how much one client is likely to spend with you over the whole time she stays. The basic formula is: average order value multiplied by orders per year multiplied by the number of years she stays.
Worked example: lifetime value for a small chops caterer

For example, Bisi runs a small chops business in Ibadan. Her average party order is about 25,000 naira (approximate). Her regular clients order about 3 times a year and typically stay with her for about 4 years.
Average order value: 25,000 naira.
Orders per year: 3. So one year is 25,000 x 3 = 75,000 naira.
Years she stays: 4. So lifetime value is 75,000 x 4 = 300,000 naira.
Bisi notices that a one-time client is worth 25,000 naira, while a loyal client is worth about 300,000 naira, twelve times as much.
If one loyal client refers just one friend who behaves the same way, that single relationship has produced about 600,000 naira of business over four years.
Bisi decides that sending a thank-you message and a reminder before the festive season is worth far more than the few minutes it takes.
Use your own numbers

Lifetime value is an estimate, not a promise. Use real figures from your sales book or WhatsApp history. If you do not know how often clients reorder yet, that is the first thing your new records will tell you.

Writing context notes that help

The most valuable field is often the free notes column, and it is also the one people fill badly. A good note is **specific, factual, dated and short**. It records what the client said or did, not your mood about her. Compare these:
Weak note
Useful note
Nice woman, buys a lot
12 Mar: ordered 3 ankara gowns for her shop. Sells mostly size 14 to 16.
Difficult
2 Apr: asked twice for delivery before Friday. Prefers updates by voice note, not text.
Has event coming
20 May: niece's wedding 14 Sept, family aso ebi for about 30 people, colour not chosen yet.

Notice that words like "difficult" or "stingy" are opinions. They do not tell your future self what to do, and if a client ever saw your records they could cause offence. Record the behaviour instead: "asked for a 10 percent discount on two orders" is a fact you can plan around.
From conversation to next action

Every time you talk to a client, finish by asking yourself: what is the next thing I should do for this person, and when? Write it in the next action field. If there is genuinely nothing, write a check-in date based on her normal buying pattern. A record without a next action is just history; a record with one becomes a plan.
Worked example: turning a chat into a record

For example, Amaka is a tailor in Enugu. A new client, Chioma, sends voice notes on 3 June asking for two office dresses. During the chat Chioma mentions she was referred by Nkechi, that she starts a new job on 1 July, and that she dislikes sleeveless styles.
Name and phone: Chioma, her WhatsApp number.
Source: referral by Nkechi. Amaka adds a note to thank Nkechi.
First order: 3 June, 2 office dresses, 36,000 naira (approximate) agreed, 18,000 naira deposit paid.
Preferences: no sleeveless; prefers knee length; voice notes rather than calls.
Important date: new job starts 1 July.
Promises made: dresses ready by 24 June, one free adjustment within two weeks.
Next action: send fitting reminder on 20 June.
In two minutes Amaka has a record that tells her exactly what to do next and gives her a natural reason to message Chioma in July to ask how the new job is going.
Write it the same day

Update the record within 24 hours of any order, delivery or meaningful conversation. After a week you will have forgotten the small details, and the small details are what make clients feel remembered.

Where the details come from

You rarely get these details in one go. Preferences appear in passing ("last time the sleeves were a bit tight"), important dates come up in small talk, and the source often comes from the first message ("Nkechi gave me your number"). Get into the habit of reading back over a chat after an order is closed and pulling out anything worth keeping. Five minutes per client, done once, saves you from scrolling through months of messages later. If a detail is unclear, ask a simple question next time you speak rather than guessing.
Only what you need

Do not record things that have nothing to do with serving her, such as her religion, health details she did not share for the order, or gossip from other clients. Keep what helps you serve her well, and nothing more. Lesson 8 covers client data privacy in detail.

Building your client tracker in Google Sheets

Add drop-down lists so status is always written the same way

In this lesson you build the tool you will use for the rest of the course. It has two tabs. **Clients** has one row per person, with her details and next action. **Orders** has one row per order, so a client who has bought eight times has eight rows there. Keeping orders separate means you never squeeze history into one cell, and Sheets can add it up for you.
Step 1: create the two tabs
Open the Google Sheets app or sheets.google.com and create a blank spreadsheet. Name it "Client tracker".
Rename the first tab "Clients". Add a second tab and name it "Orders".
In Clients, row 1, type these headings from column A to J: Client, Phone, Source, First order, Preferences, Important dates, Promises, Status, Next action, Next action date.
Add two more headings in K and L: Orders, Total spent. These will fill themselves.
In Orders, row 1, type: Date, Client, Item or service, Amount, Paid, Notes.
Freeze row 1 on both tabs (View, Freeze, 1 row) so the headings stay visible as you scroll.
A woman working on a large spreadsheet on screen
Two simple tabs, Clients and Orders, are enough to give you a real client history.
Step 2: drop-down lists for consistency

If you sometimes type "active", sometimes "Active client" and sometimes "regular", you cannot filter properly. Fix this with **data validation**. Select column H in Clients, then choose Data, Data validation, add a rule, and pick "Dropdown". Enter the options: New, Active, Quiet, Lapsed. Do the same for the Client column in Orders using "Dropdown (from a range)" pointing at Clients!A2:A, so every order is linked to a client name spelled exactly the same way.
Status
Meaning (choose your own time limits)
New
First order in the last 30 days
Active
Ordered within her normal reorder gap
Quiet
Past her normal gap but under twice the gap
Lapsed
No order for more than twice her normal gap
Step 3: let Sheets count and add

In Clients, cell K2, type =COUNTIF(Orders!B:B,A2). This counts how many rows in the Orders tab have this client's name. In L2 type =SUMIF(Orders!B:B,A2,Orders!D:D). This adds up the amounts for her orders only. Drag both cells down to the last client row. Now every new order you log updates her totals automatically.
Worked example: checking the formulas by hand

For example, Ngozi runs a home bakery in Port Harcourt. Her Orders tab has four rows for her client Ifeoma: 5 Jan 18,000 naira, 14 Feb 22,000 naira, 2 Apr 18,000 naira and 30 May 25,000 naira (all approximate).
COUNTIF looks for "Ifeoma" in column B of Orders and finds 4 rows, so K shows 4.
SUMIF adds the matching amounts: 18,000 + 22,000 + 18,000 + 25,000 = 83,000.
Ngozi checks with a calculator and gets 83,000 naira, the same as cell L.
She notices one order was typed as "Ifeoma " with a space. COUNTIF missed it until she fixed the spelling, which is why the drop-down list matters.
Ngozi trusts her totals because she tested them once by hand, and she now sees Ifeoma is one of her highest-spending clients.
Step 4: highlight overdue follow-ups

Select the range A2:L in Clients. Choose Format, Conditional formatting, and under "Format cells if" pick "Custom formula is". Type =AND($J2<>"",$J2<TODAY()) and choose a light red fill. Any client whose next action date has passed now turns red. Each morning, the red rows are your follow-up list for the day.

Common mistakes and quick fixes

**Dates typed as text:** if you type 3/6 in one row and June 3 in another, Sheets may not recognise both as dates, and the overdue highlight will fail. Select the date columns and choose Format, Number, Date so every entry is stored the same way.
**Amounts with the naira sign or commas typed in:** type 18000, not N18,000. Then use Format, Number to display it nicely. Text amounts are ignored by SUMIF.
**One client, two rows:** search the Client column before adding a new name. If a client appears twice, merge her orders under one spelling and delete the extra row.
**Formulas not copied down:** new clients added at the bottom need the COUNTIF and SUMIF formulas too. Drag the formulas a few hundred rows down in advance so they are ready.
Filter instead of scrolling
Turn on a filter (Data, Create a filter) so you can show only Quiet clients, or sort by Total spent to see your top ten. On a phone, filter views keep things readable on a small screen.
Keep the sheet private

Check the Share button: the file should be shared with no one, or only with a trusted staff member using their own Google account. Never set it to "Anyone with the link", because client phone numbers would then be visible to anyone who gets the link.

Many relationship problems start before delivery, when the client and the business understood different things. One thought "Friday" meant morning; the other meant evening. One thought the price included delivery; the other did not. A short written **order confirmation** prevents most of these arguments and gives you a record to refer back to.
The order confirmation
Send it as a WhatsApp message once the client agrees, and ask her to reply "confirmed". It should state:
What exactly she is getting (quantity, size, colour, scope of the service).
The total price, what it includes, and what it does not include (for example delivery).
Deposit amount and when the balance is due.
Delivery or completion date and time window.
What happens if she changes her mind or wants changes (for example one free adjustment within 7 days).
How and when you will update her.
Confirm payments in your bank app

Before marking an order as Paid in your tracker, check that the money has actually arrived in your bank or wallet app (for example Opay, Moniepoint or your bank). Fake transfer screenshots and fake SMS alerts are common scams. A screenshot is not proof of payment.

The after-care check is a short, specific message: "Good afternoon Mrs Okafor, I hope the trays went well at the meeting. Was the quantity right for your guests?" It shows you care about the result, not just the payment, and it often brings out feedback or a new order. Record her answer in the Notes column.
Working out when she will need you again

Many products and services repeat on a natural cycle: hair is redone every few weeks, a shop restocks every month, a child's lesson fees are due each term. Your Orders tab already shows each client's cycle. The **reorder gap** is the average number of days between her orders. To find it, take the days between her first and last order and divide by the number of gaps (one less than the number of orders).
Worked example: a reorder reminder for a shop client
For example, Funmi supplies 4-litre kegs of liquid soap to Halima, who runs a provisions shop. Halima's orders were on 3 Feb, 1 Mar, 4 Apr and 2 May.
Days from 3 Feb to 2 May: 25 days left in February, plus 31 in March, 30 in April and 2 in May = 88 days.
Halima has 4 orders, so 3 gaps. 88 divided by 3 is about 29 days.
Funmi sets the reminder a few days before the gap ends: 2 May plus 26 days is 28 May.
On 28 May she messages: "Good morning Halima, your last soap delivery was 2 May. Shall I bring the usual 6 kegs on Friday?"
If no order comes within twice the gap (about 58 days), Halima's status becomes Quiet, then Lapsed, and Funmi plans a different kind of check-in.
Halima is reminded before she runs out, so she does not buy from another supplier just because Funmi was not there at the right moment.

WhatsApp Business tools that help

The WhatsApp Business app comes with default **labels** such as New customer, New order, Pending payment, Paid and Order complete, and you can add your own, for example "After-care due" or "Reorder soon". Long-press a chat to add a label, then use the chat filter to see all chats with that label. **Quick replies** let you save a message you send often, such as your order confirmation, and insert it by typing a forward slash and a shortcut word. Always personalise the name and details before sending.
Keeping the confirmation short and friendly

A confirmation does not need to sound like a legal contract. Six short lines are enough. Here is an example a tailor might send: "Thank you Chioma. Confirming: 2 office dresses, knee length, sleeves, fabric supplied by you. Total 36,000 naira, deposit 18,000 received, balance on collection. Ready Tuesday 24 June after 2pm. One free adjustment within 7 days. I will send you a photo when they are ready. Please reply 'confirmed'." Save a version like this as a quick reply and change the details each time. When the client replies, you have a clear written record of what both of you agreed, which you can point to calmly if there is ever a disagreement about price, date or style.
How often is too often?

A useful rule: one message per stage of an order, and between orders, no more than one non-sales message a month unless the client starts the conversation. Watch her replies: short or no replies over several messages mean you should space them out.

Asking for feedback

Ask after a completed order, or every few months for regular clients. Keep it to two or three questions so it takes under a minute. You can ask directly in WhatsApp or make a free Google Form and send the link. Good questions are specific and open:
"What is one thing I do that you would not want me to change?"
"What is one thing that would make ordering from me easier?"
"On a scale of 0 to 10, how likely are you to recommend me to a friend?"

The last question is the basis of the **Net Promoter Score (NPS)**, a widely used measure created by Fred Reichheld and Bain and Company. Clients who answer 9 or 10 are **promoters**, 7 or 8 are **passives**, and 0 to 6 are **detractors**. NPS is the percentage of promoters minus the percentage of detractors. It ranges from minus 100 to plus 100.
Worked example: calculating NPS for a tutoring service
For example, Ruth runs home lessons for primary school pupils in Lagos and asks 20 parents the 0 to 10 question at the end of term.
12 parents answer 9 or 10: promoters. 12 out of 20 is 60 percent.
5 parents answer 7 or 8: passives. They are not used in the formula.
3 parents answer 6 or lower: detractors. 3 out of 20 is 15 percent.
NPS = 60 minus 15 = 45.
Ruth reads the written answers from the three detractors. Two mention that lesson times changed without notice.
Ruth's score is 45, and more importantly she has a specific fix: give parents at least a week's notice of any schedule change, and write this rule into her confirmation message.
Small numbers move a lot
With only 20 answers, one parent changing from 6 to 9 moves NPS by 15 points. Treat the score as a rough guide and track it over time. The written comments are usually more useful than the number.

Your tracker holds names, phone numbers, addresses, spending and sometimes personal details your clients shared in trust. Treating that information carefully is both ethical and a legal duty. Nigeria's **Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023** set up the **Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC)** and lays down principles for anyone who collects or uses personal data. Very small businesses may not have formal registration duties, but the principles are good practice for everyone, and clients trust businesses that follow them.
The principles in plain language
**Have a fair reason and be open about it:** collect details to serve the client, and tell her what you keep them for.
**Use it only for that purpose:** a number given for delivery should not be added to someone else's marketing list.
**Keep only what you need:** you need her delivery area, not her salary.
**Keep it accurate:** correct wrong details when you notice them.
**Do not keep it forever:** remove details of clients who ask, or who have been inactive for a long time and no longer need to be contacted.
**Keep it secure:** protect it from loss, theft and casual viewing.

The Act also gives people rights over their data, including the right to know what you hold about them and to ask for it to be corrected or deleted. If a client asks, show her what you have and act on her request. For the full text and guidance, see the NDPC website listed in this course's sources.

**Broadcast lists:** WhatsApp broadcast messages only reach people who have saved your number, which is a sign they agreed to hear from you. Still ask before adding someone: "May I send you our monthly price list?" Note the answer in her record.
**Opt-outs:** if anyone says stop, mark her record "No marketing" that same day.
**Screenshots and testimonials:** never post a client's chat, photo, face, name or number on Status or social media without her clear permission. Blur or crop names and numbers even when she agrees.
**Groups:** do not add clients to WhatsApp groups where other members can see their numbers unless they agree.
**Shared phones:** if family members use your phone, lock WhatsApp and Sheets with a fingerprint or PIN.
Honesty about capacity

Good relationships can create a new risk: more requests than you can handle well. Saying yes to everything leads to late deliveries, rushed work and broken promises, which damage the very relationships you built. Work out your real capacity and use it to decide.
Worked example: a caterer's weekly capacity

For example, Bisi cooks small chops from home in Ibadan. Besides family duties, she has about 30 working hours a week. A standard party order (about 200 pieces) takes her about 5 hours including shopping, frying, packing and delivery.
Maximum orders a week: 30 hours divided by 5 hours = 6 orders.
She keeps 1 order slot free for repeat clients' urgent requests, so she accepts up to 5 new bookings a week.
It is a busy December week: 4 orders are booked and 3 more requests arrive.
She accepts 1 (making 5), keeps the last slot for her Protect clients, and offers the other 2 people the following week.
Her message: "Thank you for thinking of me. This week is fully booked and I do not want to rush your order. I can do it next Tuesday, or I can recommend a caterer I trust."
Bisi keeps her quality and her promises. The clients she turned away were treated with respect and may book her next time.
If something goes wrong

If your phone is stolen or your WhatsApp account is taken over, act quickly. Use another phone to tell your clients on your Status or through a family member's phone that your account may be misused and that you will never ask them to send money to a new account by chat. Ask your network provider to block the SIM and retrieve your number, then re-register WhatsApp on your new phone and turn on two-step verification again. Change your Google password from another device and check which devices are signed in. Clients forgive a stolen phone; they do not forgive silence while someone uses your name to ask them for money.
Treat clients fairly

Giving loyal clients first choice of slots is fair and normal. Quietly delivering lower quality or ignoring messages from smaller clients is not. Every client should get what she was promised, even if some get extra thank-yous.

Feeling that clients are happy is not evidence. Numbers from your own records show whether your relationship work is paying off, and they make your capstone and any job application far more convincing. You need only four measures, and your tracker already holds the data.
1. Repeat client rate

**Repeat client rate** is the share of your clients who have ordered more than once. Formula: clients with 2 or more orders divided by total clients, times 100. In Google Sheets, if your Orders count is in column K, use =COUNTIF(K2:K,">=2")/COUNTA(A2:A) and format the cell as a percentage.
2. Retention rate and churn rate

**Retention rate** tells you what share of the clients you had at the start of a period you still have at the end. Use the standard formula: (clients at end of period minus new clients gained during it) divided by clients at start, times 100. **Churn rate** is the opposite: 100 minus retention. Decide what counts as still a client, for example someone who ordered at least once in the period.
Worked example: one quarter's numbers for a soap supplier
For example, Funmi reviews January to March. She counts active clients from her tracker.
Clients at start of January (S): 40.
New clients gained during the quarter (N): 12.
Clients active at end of March (E): 45.
Retention = (45 minus 12) divided by 40 = 33 divided by 40 = 0.825, so 82.5 percent.
Churn = 100 minus 82.5 = 17.5 percent. So 7 of her 40 starting clients did not order in the quarter.
Repeat rate: her list now holds 52 clients (the 40 she started with plus 12 new). 29 of them have 2 or more orders. 29 divided by 52 is about 56 percent.
Funmi now has a baseline. Next quarter she will see whether her reorder reminders and after-care checks raise retention above 82.5 percent.

Measuring repeat rate and retention each quarter shows whether your relationship work is paying off.
3. Average lifetime value

You met lifetime value in Lesson 1 as an estimate. Your tracker now gives a real figure for the past: the average of the Total spent column, =AVERAGE(L2:L). Track it each quarter. If it rises while client numbers stay the same, existing clients are buying more, which is direct evidence of stronger relationships.
4. Referrals

Your Source column already shows who came by referral. Count them with =COUNTIF(C2:C,"Referral*") (the star matches anything after the word, such as "Referral by Nkechi"). Then add up what those referred clients have spent. This shows the real value of thanking the people who recommend you.

Reading the numbers sensibly

Numbers need context. A drop in retention in January may simply follow a busy December, and a rise before Sallah or Christmas may be seasonal. She keeps 1 slot free for repeat clients' urgent requests. In a busy week, she politely offers extra requests the following week, or recommends a caterer she trusts. She keeps her quality and her promises.
Funmi measures one quarter
Start: 40 clients. New: 12. End: 45
Retention: 45 minus 12, divided by 40
That is 82.5 percent retention
Churn: 100 minus 82.5 is 17.5 percent
Repeat rate: 29 of 52, about 56 percent
Feeling that clients are happy is not evidence. Numbers are. For example, Funmi supplies soap. She started January with 40 clients, gained 12 new ones, and ended March with 45 active.
Retention is clients at the end, minus new clients, divided by clients at the start. 45 minus 12 is 33. 33 divided by 40.
That is 82.5 percent. Most of the clients she started with stayed.
Churn is the opposite: 100 minus 82.5, which is 17.5 percent.
Her repeat rate is clients with 2 or more orders, divided by all clients. 29 of 52, about 56 percent.
Count honestly. Include clients who left unhappy. A modest true number that improves beats a perfect number nobody can check.
Key points
Remember
Log promises and keep records free of blanks
Protect, Re-engage, Grow, Maintain lightly
Consent before broadcasts; honour opt-outs
Know your capacity and say no kindly
Track retention, churn, repeat rate, referrals

To remember. Keep clean records and a promises log. Review your four groups every month. Ask before marketing and honour every opt-out. Know your capacity. And track your numbers every quarter, including referrals from your Source column.

Saying I am good with clients proves nothing. Everyone says it. A short case story with real numbers convinces people.
Situation. For example, Funmi had 46 clients, but no record of who had stopped buying.
Action. She built a Google Sheets tracker, set reorder reminders from each client's buying gap, and started day-3 after-care checks.
Result. Her retention went from 82.5 percent to about 89 percent the next quarter.
She tells it three ways. For an employer, the numbers. For a partner, her reliability. For a shop client, simply: I remind you before you run out.
